Back in January week I NEEDED to fly back to Philadelphia to pack my ski bags (at my parents home) for a quick 48 hour turnaround time to get to the Canada Rockies on Jan 10th. My goal was to fly from Spain either the 7th or 8th, and I thought it may be tricky because plane loads are still heavy from Europe back to US post holiday season. No matter, I set my trusty seatsDOTaero text alert for MAD/BCN -> PHL (American Airlines is the only carrier that flies direct and they are notoriously hard to book with). I thought that there was a chance Alaska would list 1 or 2 biz class seats for this route, even though the Expert Flyer seat maps were showing very full. That being said, I also set alerts for all of Europe back to Philadelphia, and I was fully prepped to take a positioning flight from Spain to a Major EUR airport to catch the flight back. LOW AND MOTHER FCKING BEHOLD, I got an alert text this morning that there is 1 biz class seat open on Etihad (AA partner) for 80,000 points, direct to Philly! But hold on there, I know thanks to the Alliance and Transfer Partner sheet we have inside Phantom Community, Alaska is also a partner with AA and Etihad. So I run a manual check, and boom. 55,000 point biz class. This isn't rocket science. Most of the time when a partner airline such as Etihad is showing availability, others will too. The reason Alaska is better of course, is their biz class partner flights are priced AMAZINGLY, and its refundable if you need to cancel or change your date. No brainer. Did the clutch Amex - Hawaiian -> Alaskan transfer and called it a day. $4,250 flight for 55,000 pts, a nice $0.08 per point redemption. British Airways and the City of Joburg: Same Failure, Just 35,000 Feet Apart Last week, British Airways cancelled my flight. I wasn’t surprised. The signs were there, I even flagged it to them in advance. Their response? “We’ll deal with it if it happens.” And when it did, they failed. UK Regulation 261 is crystal clear: when an airline cancels your flight, they must rebook you in comparable conditions at the earliest opportunity — even if that means putting you on a rival carrier. BA offered me two entirely unsuitable options, then left me to fight for what the law already guarantees. I spent 45 minutes on the phone with an agent who outright lied to me — claiming UK261 “doesn’t apply,” that I didn’t understand the law, and that he couldn’t book me on non-partner airlines. Twice I asked to speak to a manager. Twice I was brushed off. And then — suddenly — a suitable Lufthansa flight was found. Nothing changed in the law. Just their willingness to follow it. This is what British Airways has become: a company that charges premium fares, then treats customers with disdain. They’ve gutted their customer service, monetised every element of the experience, and now hide behind policy to deny even basic accountability. You pay for first-class values and receive budget airline behaviour. And that same broken model — high input, zero output, maximum deflection — is exactly what we’re living through in Johannesburg. Yesterday, the MMC for Finance delivered the City’s budget speech. And while the language was polished, the subtext was clear: the suburbs have had their turn. Future investment, she implied, must now go elsewhere. There was no mention of the reality on the ground — that suburban infrastructure in Johannesburg hasn’t seen serious investment in over 30 years. That our water systems are decaying. That our substations are overloading. That roads and pavements are breaking down. Instead, the ANC-deployed cadres running the City’s finances speak as if these communities are already being "served" — and should now simply keep paying more for less. This is the core issue: the very residents who fund the City are treated not as stakeholders, but as cash cows. There's no reciprocity. No fairness. Just rising rates, degrading service, and a cold political message: “You’ll survive. Others need more.” In both systems — British Airways and the City of Johannesburg — we see the same pattern. The people keeping the system afloat are treated with disdain. They’re expected to pay up — premium rates, premium fares — for zero value. And any hope of accountability has vanished. Pittsburghese, or Western Pennsylvania English, is a distinct American dialect centered in Pittsburgh, known for unique vocabulary (like "yinz" for you all, "buggy" for shopping cart, "jimmies" for sprinkles) and pronunciation influenced by Scots-Irish, German, Slavic, and other immigrant groups, creating a mix of unique phrases and an iconic, often nasal, accent with terms like "nebby" (nosy) and "needs fixed". Key Features •Vocabulary: Words like "dahntahn" (downtown), "red up" (clean up), "clicker" (remote), and "slippy" (slippery) are common. •Pronunciation: A unique nasal quality, particularly in vowels, with a distinctive "ah" sound, and mergers like "cot" and "caught". •Grammar: Usage of "whenever" for specific times ("Whenever I get home...") and the "needs fixed" construction ("The car needs washed"). •Influences: A blend of Scots-Irish, German, Slavic, African American, and even Old Norse, from waves of immigration. •Identity: Strongly associated with the working-class community, with speakers called "Yinzers," and celebrated through local culture like t-shirts and media. Examples •Yinz: "Yinz wanna go for a buggy ride?" (You all want to go for a shopping cart ride?). •Red up: "I gotta red up the house." (I have to clean up the house). •Jimmies: "Put some jimmies on that ice cream." (Put sprinkles on that ice cream). Air France has announced that starting in the summer of 2025, it will begin offering high-speed WiFi on select flights through a partnership with Starlink. This service will gradually be introduced across various routes, including regional ones, and will be complimentary for all passengers. The WiFi service aims to replicate the connectivity experience one would expect on the ground, allowing passengers to maintain communication, keep up with news, engage in online gaming, and stream media during their flight. The service will support multiple device connections per passenger, accessible via smartphones, tablets, and laptops. To use the WiFi, passengers will need to log in with their Flying Blue account, though first-class travelers can access it directly without login. For those without an account, one can be created at no cost after boarding. This initiative comes alongside Air France's recent decision to experiment with a paid à la carte meal service on certain European routes, moving away from complimentary in-flight meals. The connectivity will be provided by Starlink's extensive network of low-earth orbit satellites, which ensures wide coverage, with the exception of areas where internet use is restricted. This follows similar moves by airlines like Hawaiian Airlines, which started its Starlink service in February 2024, and United Airlines, which has partnered with SpaceX for similar purposes.

Ever feel like your house is in a flight simulator? You're not alone. Let’s talk airplane noise. It’s one of those things people either shrug off or passionately debate like pineapple on pizza or whether socks belong with sandals. But for some of us, it’s not just a background hum... it’s a full-blown soundtrack to our lives. Now, before anyone jumps in with “Didn’t you know there was an airport when you bought your house?” Yes, I did. But here’s the thing: noise is a symptom, not the root cause. It’s like having a fever, it tells you something’s up. And lately, something is up. My Noise vs. Your Noise I live in a low flyover zone about 3.5 miles from the airport. I’ve lived in three different homes in this area since 2014, and I swear the noise has changed, especially in the last two years. It’s not just louder; it’s different. The recent United expansion got me curious, so I started digging into the data. I’ve compiled a report for September 2025 using info from the airport’s own monitoring tools. This focuses on my area, using readings from monitors along the departure and arrival routes. If you live near Black Rail Road or Vista Fire Station #5, you’d need to check your own local data to see how it compares. Tools You Can Use • Noise Dashboard: Created by the San Marcos PAAC rep (with help from the airport manager, I suspect), this dashboard is a goldmine for noise nerds like me. You can explore real data and trends here: 👉 Noise Dashboard: https://t.co/BnWHVAwT1Y • WebTrak: Want to know what just roared over your house? WebTrak lets you track flights and noise levels. There’s a 15–30-minute delay, so jot down the time you heard it and use the replay feature. 👉 WebTrak: https://t.co/BVExdCFbNv What’s That Sound? Let’s break it down: • Small Prop Planes: These are the quiet buzzers. Unless they’re doing aerial acrobatics or having a bad day, they’re barely noticeable. Think of them as the Prius of the skies. • Turboprops: These guys sound like angry weed whackers. They can hit 70–75 dB, which is loud enough to pause a conversation or make your dog give you the side-eye. • Midsize Jets: Your typical business-class birds. They hum like a small industrial machine and get louder as they approach. Not ear-shattering, but definitely noticeable. • Big Jets (JSX, AA, etc.): These are the heavy hitters. JSX jets average around 75 dB over my neighborhood, and American Airlines jets can hit 80 dB—comparable to a Harley or a loud air compressor. Not dangerous for your hearing in short bursts, but enough to spike your blood pressure or make you forget what you were saying. • Aggressive Maneuvers: My personal least favorite. These sudden, loud flyovers feel like the sky is yelling at you. They’ve become more frequent, possibly due to air traffic control managing tighter flight paths. I’ve started documenting these in hopes someone can help figure out a solution. What the Data Says I’ve attached a summary of this month’s WebTrak report. Over the past three months, noise events have increased by 15% compared to last year, with September alone up 9% over September 2024. But here’s the kicker: complaints have skyrocketed, especially since the new monitor was installed near Loker Ave. Vista went from 4 to 197 complaints. San Marcos, despite being one of the most impacted areas, shows fewer complaints. Why? Maybe the complaint system doesn’t recognize our addresses (I’ve tried!), or maybe we’re a windows-shut, grin-and-bear-it kind of crowd. I live about 1,200 feet from the monitor and hear planes often. Most don’t bother me, except those dive-bombers. Those are next-level annoying. Final Thought Noise isn’t just about volume, it’s about impact. If you’ve noticed changes or have insights into the odd data trends, I’d love to hear from you. Let’s keep the conversation going (when the jets aren’t interrupting us).

The pass was terminated in 2008 due to alleged misuse. Rothstein was a Chicago entrepreneur, made an audacious purchase. For $250,000, he bought American Airlines’ AAirpass, a lifetime ticket that allowed unlimited first class travel with no blackout dates. At the time, the airline viewed the program as a clever way to generate quick cash from wealthy customers who were unlikely to fly constantly. That assumption turned out to be spectacularly wrong. Over the next twenty one years, Rothstein practically lived on airplanes. He booked and flew more than 10,000 flights, sometimes hopping between cities multiple times a day. Because the pass guaranteed first class seats, he routinely flew on some of the most expensive routes in the network without paying another cent. Internal estimates later suggested his flying cost American Airlines roughly $21 million in lost revenue. By 2008, American Airlines had had enough. The company terminated Rothstein’s pass, accusing him of violating the agreement by booking speculative flights he did not intend to take and misusing companion privileges. Rothstein publicly denied wrongdoing and disputed the airline’s interpretation of the contract. Despite the controversy, there was no dramatic courtroom resolution. The pass was never reinstated, and no detailed settlement or ruling was made public. The dispute simply faded, with the airline keeping its decision intact. The fallout permanently reshaped airline thinking. American had already stopped selling AAirpasses in the early 1990s, but Rothstein’s case became the definitive cautionary tale inside the industry. What seemed like a harmless lifetime perk in the 1980s proved financially dangerous once airlines gained better data on customer behavior. Only a few dozen AAirpasses were ever sold, and none remain valid today... © Reddit #archaeohistories

When One Seat Goes Viral, It Exposes an Industry Problem” A short video showing generous legroom on a WestJet flight out of Edmonton went viral for a simple reason: people were shocked that economy class could still look humane. That reaction says more about today’s airline industry than about one airplane seat. Passengers have been conditioned to expect shrinking legroom, extra fees for basic comfort, and cabins designed more for revenue optimization than human dignity. So when a single seat offers space to breathe, stretch, and exist without apology, it feels like an exception—almost a miracle. This was likely an exit row or a specific aircraft configuration, not a system-wide policy change. But that’s precisely the point. Comfort has been elevated to a privilege, rather than a standard. Airlines sell “extra” legroom as if dignity were a luxury add-on rather than a baseline expectation. The viral video didn’t celebrate WestJet. It exposed how low the bar has fallen. When basic comfort becomes newsworthy, the industry should ask itself a hard question: When did treating passengers like cargo become normal? Because people aren’t asking for first class. Domestic US Flights: Adding an infant is free. Final Tips: Always check the infant ticket policy of both the ticket issuer and the operating airline before booking. @Turbinetraveler Iet me think this through out loud, the way I do when I’m alone at 3 a.m. staring at old photos of G-BOAF on the runway at Filton. First, the crash. Air France 4590, 25 July 2000. A strip of metal on the runway, a burst tyre, a fuel tank ripped open, fire, 113 dead. Horrible. Unforgivable in the sense that it was preventable. The investigation was brutal in its honesty: the tank design had a known vulnerability, the spacer strips between the ply layers in the tyres were missing on some wheels, runway debris discipline at CDG was lax. The fixes came fast—Kevlar liners in the tanks, better tyres, Michelin NZGs that wouldn’t shred the same way, FOD walks on runways, even little deflectors ahead of the gear. By 2001 the fleet was back in the air, certificates renewed. And people flew. Loads were solid. Celebrities, bankers, the merely rich who wanted New York breakfast and London dinner. I’ve talked to cabin crew from those last two years—they said the mood on board was almost defiant, like “we’re still here.” Then the numbers. This is where I start to waver. A Concorde overhaul cost roughly the same as buying a new widebody. Fuel burn was monstrous—four times a 747 per seat. The ozone scare (later mostly debunked) and the post-9/11 drop in premium travel hurt badly. Airbus announced they’d stop supporting the A300-600 airframe donor parts, and without Airbus the Type Certificate was toast. British Airways and Air France looked at the ledger and quietly concluded that even at $12,000 a ticket they were losing money on every flight once you rolled in the capital costs. But… but. Today I can drop $15–25k on a Qatar Qsuite or an Emirates first-class shower suite and barely blink, because half the cabin is paying it. London–New York business class is routinely $8–12k round-trip now, often more. The infra has improved—better runways, better ATC, quieter engines were already in development (the “Olympus 593 Mk 610” that never flew would have cut noise dramatically). Carbon brakes, fly-by-wire retrofits—none of it impossible. Expensive, yes. Absurdly so? Maybe not, if someone had really wanted it. This is where the doubt creeps in. Because no one did want it enough. Not the airlines (BA was bleeding cash post-9/11), not the manufacturers (Airbus wanted out), not the regulators (the FAA never gave full domestic overland rights anyway), and—here’s the part that stings—not the public either. We mourned her, we bought the posters, but we didn’t march in the streets or refuse to fly subsonic. We posted grainy videos on YouTube and moved on. Was it politics? In a way, yes. The loudest anti-Concorde voices were always political—green groups who hated the fuel burn, American airlines who hated the competitive threat and lobbied against overland routes, French and British governments quietly relieved to be rid of a prestige project that had become a money pit. The crash simply handed everyone the perfect excuse they were waiting for. I go back and forth. One day I’m convinced she could have been saved—re-engine with something derived from the Trent, sell 10 refurbished airframes to boutique operators for $20–30k a seat, turn her into the ultimate Veblen good. The next day I look at the maintenance logs and think, “My God, what a fragile, thirsty, noisy beast—she was a miracle we got 27 years out of her.” Maybe the truth is gentler than conspiracy and harsher than nostalgia: Concorde represented a moment when governments and companies were still willing to lose money for the way people lose money on art—because beauty and ambition mattered. That moment passed. Not because of one crash, not because of one Airworthiness Directive, but because we slowly, quietly, decided that three-and-a-half hours from London to New York wasn’t worth the poetry anymore. And yet every time I see that delta wing against a sunset, I feel the same thing I felt as a child a tug in the chest that says we gave up something irreplaceable. Not just speed.

AIRPLANE WITH DOUBLE DECKERS… for passengers Double-decker planes, or those with a multi-level cabin configuration, are primarily associated with two iconic aircraft: 1. **Boeing 747**: Known as the "Queen of the Skies," it has a partial upper deck, often used for first-class lounges or additional seating. This plane has been used by numerous countries for both passenger and cargo operations. However, its production has ceased, but it remains in service with airlines like Lufthansa and Korean Air for some passenger routes, and significantly in cargo versions by carriers like Atlas Air. - **Inside**: The upper deck of the 747 is smaller than the main cabin but often used for luxury or business class. It's like a VIP room in the sky where the elite can escape the common folk, but without the champagne fountains you'd expect in such an exclusive club. 2. **Airbus A380**: This is the full double-decker jetliner with both decks running the length of the fuselage. It's operated by airlines from countries like the UAE (Emirates), Singapore (Singapore Airlines), Australia (Qantas), and others. - **Inside**: The A380 is like a flying palace with its spacious interior. The upper deck is often where you'll find the swanky business and first-class cabins, sometimes with lounges and even shower spas, because why not freshen up at 35,000 feet? The main deck typically houses economy and premium economy. It's like having a party where the cool kids hang out upstairs, and the rest of us mingle with the snack bar downstairs. Countries where these planes operate include: - **United Arab Emirates**: Emirates is the largest operator of the A380, with Dubai International Airport as a major hub. - **Singapore**: Singapore Airlines, one of the first operators of the A380. - **France**: Air France has flown the A380, although they've been reducing their fleet. - **Germany**: Lufthansa has utilized both the A380 and 747-8 for long-haul flights. - **South Korea**: Korean Air has operated the 747 and A380 for international routes. - **Australia**: Qantas has used the A380 for routes like Melbourne to Los Angeles. The trend towards double-deckers has waned with a shift towards more fuel-efficient, twin-engine aircraft, but these giants still grace the skies in some parts of the world, offering that unique experience of flying in a plane that feels more like a vertical community than a traditional aircraft.

In 1987, cash-strapped American Airlines launched the AAirpass: $250,000 for unlimited lifetime first-class travel. Investment banker Steven Rothstein, a frequent flyer, bought one immediately. In 1989 he added a $150,000 companion pass that let anyone fly with him—even on separate flights. From 1987 to 2008, Rothstein averaged 476 flights per year (over 10,000 total, 30 million miles). He flew to London for dinner, Tokyo for sushi, Sydney for weekends—treating planes like buses. He used the companion pass for profound kindness: spotting stranded travelers, homeless people, priests, or refugees at airports and gifting them first-class seats home. His daughter said he turned the pass into a tool for random, life-changing generosity. American Airlines sold just 66 passes (1981–1988), raising $16.5 million. Early on, the CEO wrote Rothstein praising his use and promising to honor the deal “far into the future.” By 2007, facing losses, the airline created a “revenue integrity unit.” It calculated Rothstein and one other holder were each costing >$1 million yearly. From 2005–2008 he booked 3,000+ segments for himself (84% canceled/no-show) and 2,700 companion segments (85% unused). Many bookings used placeholder names (“Bag Rothstein,” “Steven Rothstein Jr.”) because he decided at the gate whom to help. Reservations were made by phone; staff knew and never objected—some even suggested the practice. On December 13, 2008, at Chicago O’Hare, while escorting a Bosnian policeman he was flying home, Rothstein was handed a letter revoking his AAirpass for “fraudulent usage.” His 21-year unlimited life ended instantly. The airline accused him of speculative bookings and fake names. Rothstein sued for breach of contract; AA countersued for fraud. The case settled confidentially in 2012 after AA’s bankruptcy. A deeper truth emerged in court: after his teenage son Josh died in 2002, many late-night bookings were grief-driven calls to familiar reservation agents—his only human contact when loneliness was unbearable. The unused tickets weren’t fraud; they were a heartbroken father staying tethered to the world. American Airlines later terminated all remaining AAirpasses. Former CEO Bob Crandall admitted: “The public was smarter than we were.” Rothstein never accepted wrongdoing but later said he had mixed feelings about ever buying the pass. It gave him freedom and the power to help thousands—yet ended in betrayal. His story is the last real unlimited lifetime airline pass: a brief era when a golden ticket actually meant forever, until corporate promises met bottom-line reality. For 10,000 flights and 30 million miles, Steven Rothstein lived—and shared—a dream that no longer exists.

L’homme qui a transformé un billet d’avion en clé du monde En 1987, Steven Rothstein, un homme d’affaires de l’Illinois, a posé un geste qui allait le faire entrer dans la légende du voyage. Pour la somme colossale de 250 000 dollars, il a acquis l’AAirpass d’American Airlines, un sésame promettant des vols illimités à vie, en première classe, vers n’importe quelle destination de la planète. Ce n’était pas seulement un achat, c’était l’acquisition d’une liberté sans frontières. Pendant plus de deux décennies, Rothstein a mené une existence hors du commun, affranchie des contraintes de temps et de distance. Son quotidien se déroulait entre les fuseaux horaires : un petit-déjeuner à New York, un déjeuner d’affaires à Londres, et un coucher de soleil à Tokyo. On estime qu’il a effectué plus de 10 000 vols, accumulant des dizaines de millions de miles, et coûtant à la compagnie aérienne une somme estimée à plus de 21 millions de dollars. Mais au-delà de l’exploit logistique et du luxe, Rothstein voyait dans cet abonnement une véritable philosophie de vie. Il voyageait parfois sans but précis, simplement pour le plaisir de voler. Mieux encore, il utilisait son privilège pour inviter des inconnus rencontrés dans les aéroports à l’accompagner en première classe, transformant son voyage en un acte de générosité spontanée. Il vivait avec la légèreté d’un oiseau, faisant du monde son voisinage. Cette utopie a pris fin brutalement en 2008. American Airlines, réalisant l’énormité de la perte financière engendrée par ces pass illimités, a cherché une porte de sortie. La compagnie a finalement annulé le pass de Rothstein, l’accusant d’en avoir “trop profité” et de pratiques frauduleuses, notamment l’utilisation de faux noms pour réserver des sièges de compagnon. Bien que la justice ait finalement donné raison à la compagnie en 2011, l’histoire de Steven Rothstein demeure un témoignage fascinant. Il reste l’homme qui a prouvé qu’il était possible, pour un temps, de faire du ciel sa véritable adresse, et dont la légende continue de voler bien au-delà de l’annulation de son billet. @ClassicsPlanes "Lockheed L-1011 TriStar. Usually spoken of in its homeland the US as either the “L-One-Oh-Eleven” or the “L-Ten-Eleven,” which was parodied in its declining years as L-Ten-a-Lemon and said to denote Late 10 out of 11 times; also the Tribastard and Frightstar. Swamp Buggy and Swamp Eater referred to the infamous Eastern 401 crash in the Everglades in 1972. Eastern included the TriStar in their Whisperliner fleet, and when introduced on Caribbean routes it was referred to there as el Grandote (The Big Guy) At PSA the widebody was the Mother Grinning Bird to complement the narrowbody Grinning Birds. Cabin crew at Delta called it the Tritanic, as a slight nose-up attitude in flight was thought reminiscent of the raised bow of a sinking ship. When first introduced into British Airways service, pilots called it the Tripod, and cabin crew allegedly knew it as the Big Dipper because of the increased opportunities for “Dipping” (transferring free First-Class spirits into miniatures for private re-sale in Economy) The “Sunset” mod at BA involved replacing the lower galley and lifts on -200s to create extra freight space. The unusual semi-circle of toilets at the rear was known within Lockheed as Cannery Row (can being US slang for a toilet) and at Caledonian as Penny Lane (“Spending a penny” being British slang for using a toilet) The aforementioned nose-up pitch combined with urine splashes was said to produce a distinctly unpleasant smell on the TriStar, and if the lids were up and thrust-reversal applied on landing the resultant sound was said to be like “gunfire.” The noise-reducing fairing below the intake of the centre engine on the -500 was known as the Frisbee, not because of any resemblance to the throwing disc but because it was devised by Lockheed’s Lloyd Frisbee. BiStar was a reference to engine failures, although it was also used more formally in relation to the unbuilt twin-engined L-1011-600 (aka the CL1600) The only military operator was the UK, who bought 6 ex British Airways L1011-500s in the immediate wake of the 1982 Falklands war, primarily for use as K.1 & KC.1 tankers; these soon became known as Tommies, possibly deriving from the rhyming slang Tommy Tanker (Wanker) A further 3 ex Pan Am -500s were ordered 2 years later as pure C.2 passenger aircraft and given the complementary name of Timmy, with the sole C.2A upgrade sometimes being referred to as Tammy. The two TriStars sent to Saudi Arabia during the first Gulf War and given ”sand pink” camouflage were known collectively as the Pink Pigs or Flying Pigs, and individually as Pinky & Perky after the children’s TV show characters. British charter operator Court Line also had a pink TriStar, G-BAAB “Halcyon Breeze” known within the company as the Pink Lady, operated alongside G-BAAA “Halcyon Days” or the Big Banana." Without institutions, without enforced norms, there’s only a fragile barrier separating civilization from the chaos of history. We get glimpses of this in war, riots, and moments of lawlessness—but for the most part, societal structure keeps people in line, adhering to an unspoken social contract. Occasionally, though, we see cracks in that structure—reminders of how thin the veil really is. My brother once told me a story about watching Brazilians check in for a flight to the United States. The scene was loud and chaotic—shouting, jostling, cutting in line—because in that environment, securing attention and getting what you need requires forcefulness. In a society where institutions are weaker, you have to act in your own interest because everyone else does. To someone from a highly structured society, this behavior seems aggressive, even rude. But within that system, it’s simply survival. Then, something remarkable happened. The same people, upon entering the first-class lounge of American Airlines in São Paulo, transformed instantly. Gone was the shouting, the shoving, the disorder. Inside the lounge, they adapted to the rules of a structured environment—a space governed by the quiet, orderly expectations of American or Canadian norms. The contrast was stark. This is why institutions matter. They don’t just impose order; they shape behavior itself. When people talk about dismantling these structures, they should tread carefully. Because when the scaffolding of society weakens, history reminds us of what waits on the other side.

Lufthansa’s decision to reactivate stored A340-600s and keep them flying—even after intending to retire the type—boils down to holding capacity for its First Class product and plugging gaps caused by delivery delays of newer aircraft. 1.Premium-cabin demand Since the pandemic recovery began, demand for First Class has rebounded more strongly than expected. At Munich, no other long-haul type besides the quadjet offered a full First-Class cabin until the new A350-900s with Allegra suites arrived. Reinstating five A340-600s in summer 2021 (and eventually all ten) allowed Lufthansa to quickly regain premium-cabin capacity without waiting for new-build deliveries. 2.Aircraft-delivery bottlenecks Lufthansa’s wide-body modernization hinges on additional Boeing 787s and A350-900 First-Class retrofits. Production and certification delays for both programmes left the airline short of long-haul seats. Rather than suffer network cuts—or deploy less-fuel-efficient 747-8s—reactivating the mothballed A340-600s provided an interim supply of long-range, four-class jets to maintain its schedule. 3.Seasonal traffic peaks Each summer, Lufthansa has cycled A340-600s between storage and service to match peak long-haul demand. In Q2 of 2021, 2022, and 2023, it brought aircraft back from Teruel and Manila for summer flying before pausing them again in quieter months. In early 2023, the carrier confirmed returning its full ten-aircraft A340-600 fleet to cover growing summer traffic from both Frankfurt and Munich hubs. 4.First Class network consistency By keeping A340-600s in use, Lufthansa can guarantee First Class availability on flagship routes to New York, Hong Kong, Bogotá and other high-yield city pairs—protecting revenue and loyalty-programme objectives until its next-generation premium cabins roll out. In short, Lufthansa’s A340-600 comeback is a strategic stopgap: it preserves Lufthansa’s premium offering and network breadth amid surging business-class demand and slower than planned arrivals of its most efficient long-haul replacements. In 1987, Steve Rothstein made a decision that seemed almost outrageous at the time: he paid \$250,000 for American Airlines’ unlimited “golden ticket,” granting him free first-class flights for life. On top of that, he purchased a \$150,000 companion pass so he could bring anyone along. For Steve, travel wasn’t about collecting miles or rewards—it was about freedom without limits, and he used it to the fullest. Over the years, Rothstein booked more than 10,000 flights, sometimes hopping on a plane just to have lunch in another state before returning home the same day. He was known for his generosity, often giving away trips to strangers, helping homeless individuals reunite with their families, or booking seats for companions who never showed up. His unusual habits made him both a legend and a financial headache, as American Airlines eventually calculated that he had cost them over \$21 million. In 2008, the airline revoked his pass, accusing him of misuse. But Rothstein fought back, pointing to the binding contract he had purchased decades earlier. The courts sided with him, and his golden ticket remained valid. Today, Steve Rothstein is remembered not only as the most extraordinary frequent flyer but also as a symbol of how one small clause in a contract can unlock the entire world. © Aviation History #archaeohistories

@Fahadnaimb Emirates: Full-Service Luxury Model, and even in economy, the cabin service and confort is from another planet👍 Emirates operates as a premium, long-haul airline focused on high-end service, comfort, and a hub-and-spoke network centered in Dubai. This requires significantly more staff per aircraft. -Large cabin crews for multi-class service — Emirates flies widebody aircraft (mostly Airbus A380s and Boeing 777s, with ~252 aircraft in service as of late 2025). Flights often feature First Class, Business Class, Premium Economy, and Economy, with amenities like onboard showers (on A380s), lounges, gourmet meals, and extensive entertainment. This demands higher crew-to-passenger ratios—typically 20+ cabin crew per flight on an A380. -Extensive ground and support staff — The Emirates Group (which includes the airline, ground handling via dnata, catering, engineering, and more) employs around 121,000–125,000 people total. Many roles support premium operations, such as dedicated lounges, chauffeurs, catering facilities, and global sales/network teams. -Long-haul operations — Fewer daily flights per aircraft but longer durations mean staff are spread across fewer cycles, and the focus is on quality over volume. Current figures (as of late 2025): ~252 passenger aircraft and ~125,000 group employees → roughly 496 employees per aircraft if including the full group, but even airline-specific staff is much higher than low-cost peers. Older data often cited ~200–250 when including group operations. Ryanair: Ultra-Low-Cost Efficiency Model Ryanair prioritizes minimal costs, high utilization, and point-to-point short-haul flights across Europe to offer the lowest fares. - Lean operations and high aircraft utilization — Ryanair's fleet (600–620 Boeing 737s in 2025) flies short routes with quick turnarounds (25–30 minutes), allowing 6+ flights per day per aircraft. This maximizes productivity with fewer planes and staff needed overall. - Minimal service and staffing — Single-class economy (high-density seating, 189–230 seats per plane), no free meals/drinks, limited amenities, and charges for extras. Cabin crews are smaller (6–8 per flight), and many functions (e.g., cleaning, check-in) are outsourced or passenger-self-service. - Focused workforce — ~26,000–27,000 employees (mostly pilots and cabin crew), with high productivity. No large ground handling/catering subsidiaries bloating numbers. - Standardization — All-Boeing 737 fleet reduces training/maintenance staff needs. Current figures: ~600+ aircraft and ~26,000 employees → ~43 employees per aircraft. Why the Ratio Differs So MuchFull-service airlines like Emirates invest heavily in passenger experience, requiring more labor-intensive operations (e.g., more crew per passenger, elaborate catering, global support). Low-cost carriers like Ryanair strip out frills, outsource where possible, and maximize aircraft/crew efficiency to keep costs (and fares) low. These ratios are rough averages and can vary by how "employees" are counted (airline-only vs. group, including contractors). The core explanation holds: service level and operational model drive the massive gap.

Reposting for Veterans Day 2025 #Veteransday https://t.co/ZS83AgL0Qm QT @JJRjrESQ: SEVEN FLIGHTS FROM THAILAND - ONE VET'S RETURN “Why are those soldiers in first class?” a business passenger on an American Airlines flight from San Francisco Int’l to O’Hare grumbled. “I had to pay for my seat.” Joining the first-class cabin were two uniformed U.S. Air Force members discharged that morning, January 25, 1970. The stewardess had escorted them up front under AA’s upgrade policy for returning military. One was Seargeant James Reardon, Sr., and he gladly sat down, saying thank you in a foreign language. At 6’1”, he was down from 180 lbs to 145. * * * This Veteran’s Day note seeks to chronicle a turning point, the days surrounding one Veteran’s discharge, marking the fulfilment of a sacrificial commitment. * * * To get this far, on January 22, 1970, Reardon and other Airmen had taken a C130 cargo plane from Udorn, Thailand AFB to Bangkok (Don Mueang Airport). The returning Airmen ate dinner, staying one night at the Vien Thi Hotel. Next, they boarded a Continental 707, affectionately, the "bird with the big brass ass” rather than the airline's slogan. Waiting during a 10-hour engine change, Reardon counseled a frustrated Army soldier, “you don’t want to be over the ocean if this goes out.” He had seen a few planes skid off the Udorn runway. On January 23, 1970, the freedom bird back to “the World” took off Easterly, refueling in the Philippines, Guam, and Hawaii, landing on the 24th at Travis AFB, San Francisco. Expected to take up to 3 nights in unaccommodating “transient Airmen” barracks, he learned at 5 am they would be discharged on January 25. While Reardon’s papers were initially missing, he was third or fourth out. The Air Force gave a speech about not being able to enlist for 90 days: some groaned and some cried with laughter. With $700 for remaining pay and a flight, from Travis, you were on your own. Leaving Travis AFB, he and some other Airmen took a cab to San Francisco Int'l to find flights. He was able to book a standby flight to Chicago O’Hare with no time to call home. From San Francisco, Reardon enjoyed the warm towel and first-class meal. At O’Hare, he needed to find another standby ticket to Hartford. He called his wife to say he would arrive at Bradley at midnight. Reardon’s parents, 13 y/o sister, wife and son headed in anticipation to Bradley. It was snowing and the sidewalks were like glass. Waiting at the arrival gate, midnight came and went and they were hearing the plane was cancelled. They began to leave, when they heard a page over the intercom. "Paging Beth Reardon.” Reardon told her that he was at Logan. The plane had been diverted on its descent. He also told her that a bus was to take him to Springfield, which turned out to be incorrect. Unaware, the welcome party packed up taking an icy Route 91 North to the Springfield bus station. Reardon took a seat on the bus, and was now told it would go to Bradley—no stops. The driver refused to stop anywhere along the way, invoking Reardon’s ire, who stepped off to hitchhike in the snowfall. He found a convenience store, took a cardboard box and a marker and wrote, “Springfield.” The dress uniform wasn’t much comfort in the cold—though much better than his lightweight 1505’s. AA had lost his luggage, a heavy blue B4 duffel. The first ride took him to the entrance ramps of the toll booths of the Mass. Pike. In the meantime, his family gave up on the bus, and headed home. Next, a pickup truck, with a friendly man took him to the Palmer rest area, now closed. From a pay phone, he called his brother Raymond, a steamfitter, who in his signature gravelly voice said, “I knew I would have to come and get you.” Now 3:30 am Monday, Reardon responded, “If you can’t give me a ride, give me someone else’s phone number.” Ray met him at 5 a.m. Heading West and getting off old Exit 4 (now 45), passing the Turnpike sign with a Pilgrim hat with an arrow through it, they were home, almost. He was still “keyed up”, being 12 hours ahead. Instead of going directly home, they went to Uncle Milties in Holyoke for coffee. He wanted a moment to acclimate before re-entering civilian atmosphere. Reardon took a table and brother Ray went to the counter. The clerk was pointing in Seargeant Reardon’s direction. Ray told him the clerk wants to know why you are in uniform. “Really, I am in the Air Force. That’s why.” His mother had told him his return should be low key in part because of the anti-war “people.” Ray let him out at the apartment. He could not believe the snow banks. He had not met his 7-month-old daughter, and his son (born while Reardon was stationed at Dover AFB) was now 21 months. True, the Airforce had offered a visit when his daughter was born; he was not sure he would be able to go back. His wife, who had moved in with her conservative Jewish parents during the 11-month Udorn tour, had set up their new apartment. The dining room would serve as the second bedroom with saloon doors between the living room. Weekly rent was $12.50, with a budget to the penny on a new nurse’s salary. His wife also had taken care of his community college applications. Walking up the stairs, his wife came down from the third floor to meet him on that fateful second floor landing. Crying, she had slept in the red dress from the night before so she would have it on when he arrived. His mother and sister had slept on the couch. He took a bath and slept for 10 hours. When he woke up, he met his daughter, and his son didn’t recognize him. In two days, classes started. The B4 bag ultimately was delivered. A day late, they had a small welcome home party. Traditional Irish hors d'ouevres, potato chips and onion dip. Seven flights for cold beer and kielbasa. Coming home to the World. It was perfect. * * * In the first hours of his return, this honorably discharged member of the Air Force experienced interactions of gratefulness, jealousy, helpfulness, and disdain. Today, many take the service of Veterans for granted. As for that first-class seat, rest assured, it wasn’t free.
